\chapter{The First Verbs}
\label{ch:it-first-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build my own Italian sentences with -are verbs and drop the subject pronoun the way Italians do.}

Conjugate parlare, abitare and lavorare across io, tu and lui with no pronoun spoken, then answer for yourself what you speak, where you live and where you work.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[parlare]{parlare — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} the model -are verb}

\label{lesson:IT-C05-parlare}



\begin{quote}
Until now you've assembled fixed phrases. \textbf{parlare} (\textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is your first real \textbf{verb} and the model for Italian's largest \textbf{-are} family. Learn this pattern and you drive thousands.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — a single tapped \emph{r}: \textbf{parlare} = \emph{par-LA-reh}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-open} — clean open \emph{ah} vowels.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{parlare} comes from Late Latin \textbf{parabolāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to tell parables, to discourse\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{parabola}, \textquotedblleft{}a comparison, a speech\textquotedblright{} (Greek \emph{parabolē}). So to \emph{speak} is, at root, to \emph{tell parables}. The English family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parable}, \textbf{parole} (a word of honour), \textbf{palaver}, \textbf{parley}, \textbf{parliament} (a \emph{talking}-place).
\end{itemize}

And a lovely cross-link: \textbf{Italian \emph{parlare} and French \emph{parler} are the same word} — both from \emph{parabolāre}. \textbf{Spanish went a different way}: its \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{hablar}, is from \emph{fabulārī} (\textquotedblleft{}to chat,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fābula} $\to$ fable). So Italy and France \textquotedblleft{}tell parables\textquotedblright{}; Spain \textquotedblleft{}tells fables.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -are present tense (and pro-drop)}]
Drop \textbf{-are} to get \emph{parl-}, then add the endings:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{\emph{parlare} $\to$} \\
\midrule
(io) & \textbf{-o} & \textbf{parlo} (I speak) \\
(tu) & \textbf{-i} & \textbf{parli} (you speak) \\
(lui/lei) & \textbf{-a} & \textbf{parla} (he/she speaks) \\
(noi) & -iamo & parliamo \\
(voi) & -ate & parlate \\
(loro) & -ano & parlano \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Like Spanish (\emph{hablo/hablas}), \textbf{Italian drops the subject pronoun} — \emph{parlo} already says \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} so you don't need \emph{io}. This closes a neat circle you've been building:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Drop the pronoun}: Spanish (\emph{hablo}), \textbf{Italian (\emph{parlo})} — endings are distinct.
  \item \textbf{Keep the pronoun}: French (\emph{je parle} — endings silent), German (\emph{ich wohne} — grammar needs a subject).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}parlare\textquotedblright{} — \emph{par-LA-reh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}parlo, parli, parla\textquotedblright{} — no \emph{io} needed
  \item parlare / parler (same \emph{parabolāre}) vs Spanish \emph{hablar} (\emph{fabulārī})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gives \emph{parlare}, and which French verb is its twin? (\emph{parabolāre} — French \emph{parler}.) Which Romance \textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{} verb is from a \emph{different} root, and which? (Spanish \emph{hablar} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fabulārī}.) Does Italian keep or drop \emph{io}, and why? (Drops it — the endings are distinct.) Next: \textbf{abitare}, \textquotedblleft{}to live.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[abitare]{abitare — \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} about \emph{having a place}}

\label{lesson:IT-C05-abitare}



\begin{quote}
A second \textbf{-are} verb — snap it into the endings you just learned. \textbf{abitare} (\textquotedblleft{}to live, to dwell\textquotedblright{}) lets you say \emph{where} you live — and it's the twin of French \emph{habiter}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{abitare} = \emph{a-bee-TA-reh} (Italian dropped the Latin \emph{h-}, but the spelling and sense stayed). Clean open vowels, tapped \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{abitare} comes from Latin \textbf{habitāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to dwell, to keep having {[}a place{]}\textquotedblright{}} — the \textbf{frequentative} of \textbf{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{} To \emph{dwell} is to \emph{keep having} your place. The English family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{habitat} — where a creature dwells; \textbf{inhabit}, \textbf{inhabitant}, \textbf{habitation}.
  \item via \emph{habēre} (\textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{habit} (what you keep having), \textbf{able}, \textbf{ability}.
\end{itemize}

French kept the \emph{h} in spelling (\emph{habiter}); Italian dropped it (\emph{abitare}) — same Latin verb, same meaning. Now you can answer a \emph{dove} (\textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}) question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Abito a Roma.} — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Rome.\textquotedblright{} (No \emph{io} — pro-drop.)
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same -are template}]
| (io) abito · (tu) abiti · (lui/lei) abita | (-o / -i / -a) |

| abitiamo · abitate · abitano |  |

Identical to \emph{parlare} — nothing new. That's the whole point of a regular pattern.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}abitare\textquotedblright{} — \emph{a-bee-TA-reh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}abito, abiti, abita\textquotedblright{} — same endings as \emph{parlo/parli/parla}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Abito a Roma\textquotedblright{}; and \textquotedblleft{}abitare\textquotedblright{} $\leftrightarrow$ English \emph{habitat}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{abitare} from, and what does it literally involve? (\emph{habitāre} — \textquotedblleft{}keep having a place,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{}) English cousins? (Habitat, inhabit.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I live in Rome.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Abito a Roma.}) Next: \textbf{lavorare}, \textquotedblleft{}to work.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lavorare]{lavorare — \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} the honest kind}

\label{lesson:IT-C05-lavorare}



\begin{quote}
A third \textbf{-are} verb — and a satisfying twist. Where Spanish and French built their word for \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} out of \textbf{torture}, \textbf{Italian took a different road entirely}: \emph{lavorare}, from plain Latin \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to labour.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lavorare} = \emph{la-vo-RA-reh}: clean vowels, tapped \emph{r}. (The \emph{v} is a real \emph{v}, unlike Spanish.)
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lavorare} comes from Latin \textbf{labōrāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to labour, to work, to strive\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{labor}, \textquotedblleft{}toil, effort.\textquotedblright{} No torture device here; just honest labour. The English family is large and dignified:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{labor / labour}, \textbf{laborious}, \textbf{laboratory} (a \emph{working}-place).
  \item \textbf{elaborate} (\textquotedblleft{}worked \emph{out}\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{collaborate} (\textquotedblleft{}labour \emph{together}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

Here's the cross-language payoff — the same idea, \textbf{two very different roots}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{from} & \textbf{literal picture} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Italian} & \emph{lavorare} & \emph{labōrāre} & \textbf{labour, effort} \\
\textbf{Spanish} & \emph{trabajar} & \emph{tripalium} & \textbf{a torture rack} \\
\textbf{French} & \emph{travailler} & \emph{tripalium} & \textbf{a torture rack} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spain and France remember work as \emph{torture} ($\to$ \emph{travail/travel}); Italy remembers it as \emph{labour}. A single glance at three verbs, and you see two Roman attitudes to a day's work.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same -are template}]
| (io) lavoro · (tu) lavori · (lui/lei) lavora | (-o / -i / -a) |

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Lavoro a Milano.} — \textquotedblleft{}I work in Milan.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lavorare\textquotedblright{} — \emph{la-vo-RA-reh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lavoro, lavori, lavora\textquotedblright{}
  \item Italian \emph{lavorare} (labour) vs Spanish \emph{trabajar} / French \emph{travailler} (torture)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{lavorare} from, and its English cousins? (\emph{labōrāre} — labor, laboratory, elaborate.) How does its root differ from Spanish \emph{trabajar} and French \emph{travailler}? (Those are from \emph{tripalium}, \textquotedblleft{}torture\textquotedblright{}; Italian is from \emph{labor}, \textquotedblleft{}toil.\textquotedblright{}) Say \textquotedblleft{}I work in Milan.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Lavoro a Milano.}) Next: your first sentence — \textbf{Parlo italiano}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Parlo italiano]{Parlo italiano — your first real sentence}

\label{lesson:IT-C05-parlo-italiano}



\begin{quote}
The moment it pays off: you take a \textbf{verb} you conjugated and a \textbf{noun}, and build a sentence no one handed you — \emph{Parlo italiano}, \textquotedblleft{}I speak Italian.\textquotedblright{} (Italian \emph{parlo} covers both \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I am speaking.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: italiano}
\textbf{italiano} = \textquotedblleft{}Italian,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{Italia} — the ancient name of the peninsula itself. Its own origin is delightfully humble: many scholars trace \emph{Italia} to Oscan \textbf{víteliú}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}land of calves / young cattle\textquotedblright{}} (kin to Latin \emph{vitulus}, \textquotedblleft{}calf,\textquotedblright{} and perhaps English \emph{veal}). So \emph{Italia} may literally have meant \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Calf-land.\textquotedblright{}} Say it \emph{ee-ta-LYA-no}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the assembled sentence}
Snap two things you own together:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Parlo} (I speak, from \emph{parlare}) + \textbf{italiano} (Italian) = \textbf{Parlo italiano.}
\end{quote}

A complete, grammatical Italian sentence. Notice what's \emph{not} there:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{No \emph{io}.} Italian drops it (like Spanish \emph{hablo español}) — the \emph{-o} of \emph{parlo} already says \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Io parlo italiano} is fine for emphasis only.
  \item \textbf{No article} on the language: \emph{parlo italiano}.
\end{itemize}

This closes the \textbf{pronoun-rule circle} you've watched across five languages:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{pronoun} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
Spanish / Italian & \textbf{dropped} & \emph{hablo/parlo}: distinct endings \\
\textbf{French} \emph{je parle} & kept & endings are silent \\
\textbf{German} \emph{ich lerne} & kept & grammar needs an overt subject \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Swap the pieces: \textbf{Abito a Roma.} · \textbf{Lavoro a Milano.} · \textbf{Parli italiano?}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Parlo italiano\textquotedblright{} — \emph{PAR-lo ee-ta-LYA-no}
  \item drop the \emph{io} — Italian doesn't need it (like Spanish, unlike French)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}italiano\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{Italia}, maybe \textquotedblleft{}calf-land\textquotedblright{} — a humble, farmerly name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{italiano} come from, and what might \emph{Italia} have meant? (\emph{Italia}; perhaps \textquotedblleft{}land of calves.\textquotedblright{}) In \emph{Parlo italiano}, why no \emph{io} and no article? (The \emph{-o} ending is \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}; languages take no article.) Which two of the five languages \emph{drop} the pronoun? (Spanish and Italian.) Next: practice.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — making sentences with -are verbs}

\label{lesson:IT-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
For the first time you're \textbf{building} Italian sentences from a pattern, not reciting phrases. Drill the three verbs until the endings are automatic — and remember, Italian drops the \emph{io}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: conjugate on command}]
Run each through \emph{io / tu / lui-lei} (pronoun dropped in speech):

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parlare}: parlo · parli · parla
  \item \textbf{abitare}: abito · abiti · abita
  \item \textbf{lavorare}: lavoro · lavori · lavora
\end{itemize}

Same endings every time (\textbf{-o / -i / -a}), and no pronoun needed.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: say something real}]
\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Parli} italiano? — Sì, \textbf{parlo} un po'. E tu? — Anch'io. \textbf{Dove abiti}? — \textbf{Abito} a Roma, e \textbf{lavoro} a Milano. — Grazie! — Prego.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the regular -are present tense} — drop \emph{-are}, add \emph{-o/-i/-a/-iamo/-ate/-ano}; the pronoun is \textbf{dropped} (like Spanish).
  \item \textbf{parlare} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{parabolāre} $\to$ parable; = French \emph{parler}, vs Spanish \emph{hablar}), \textbf{abitare} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{habitāre} $\to$ habitat; twin of \emph{habiter}), \textbf{lavorare} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{labōrāre} $\to$ labor/laboratory — the \textquotedblleft{}labour\textquotedblright{} road, not Spanish/French \textquotedblleft{}torture\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{Parlo italiano} — first self-assembled sentence (\emph{italiano} $\leftarrow$ \emph{Italia}, perhaps \textquotedblleft{}calf-land\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{The pronoun circle across 5 languages}: ES \emph{hablo} + IT \emph{parlo} \textbf{drop}; FR \emph{je parle} (silent endings) + DE \emph{ich lerne} (grammar) \textbf{keep}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item conjugate all three verbs, io/tu/lui — no pronoun spoken
  \item answer about yourself — what you speak, where you live, where you work
  \item chain it — \textquotedblleft{}Ciao! Parlo italiano. Parli italiano? … Arrivederci!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Parli italiano? — Sì, parlo un po'.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three singular \emph{-are} endings? (\emph{-o / -i / -a}.) Give the \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms of the three verbs. (\emph{Parlo, abito, lavoro}.) Which languages drop the subject pronoun, and which keep it, and why? (Drop: ES/IT — distinct endings; keep: FR — silent endings, DE — grammar.) Italian now moves in real sentences.
\end{tcolorbox}
